analysis.one_liner: Lets tenants in federally subsidized buildings withhold rent, force repairs, and sue to enforce housing standards.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in June 2024 and referred to the House Financial Services Committee, where it stayed until the 118th Congress ended — no vote was ever taken.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would give tenants in federally subsidized apartment buildings real tools when landlords let conditions slide: tenants could pay their rent into an escrow account instead of to the landlord until HUD-verified violations are fixed, pay for repairs themselves and deduct the cost from rent, and could not be evicted for doing so. It would also let tenants petition for inspections, get the building's ownership and inspection records from HUD, and sue to enforce their building's federal agreements if HUD ignores them. None of this happened: the bill sat in the House Financial Services Committee until the 118th Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: The roughly 1.5 million households in federally assisted multifamily rental housing — seniors, disabled people, and low-income families whose rent is subsidized — gain the practical power to force repairs, withhold rent into escrow, trigger inspections, and see the financial records of their landlords. Independent tenant organizations gain a funded grant program for organizing and training. Tenants' everyday living conditions are the direct stake; the mechanism works by putting federal subsidy dollars on the line whenever a building fails inspections.

how_it_helps.text: Lets tenants in federally subsidized multifamily housing withhold their rent share into an escrow account when HUD finds serious housing-standard violations, and bars owners from evicting them for doing so.
Lets tenants pay for repairs themselves — up to a month's gross rent — and deduct the cost from their rent.
Lets HUD or local housing agencies withhold subsidies from problem landlords, freeze their rent increases, or take over management of the building to force repairs.
Allows tenants to request inspections directly: a petition from 25% of tenants, or a request from local government, triggers a HUD inspection or management review.
Gives residents standing to enforce their building's federal agreements in court if HUD does not act on a petition within 90 days — or 15 days where health and safety are threatened.

Requires HUD to disclose ownership entities, operating statements, subsidy contracts, inspection reports, and escrow balances for a building to a legitimate residents association, so tenants can see who owns the property and how it is being run.

Funds tenant organizing and training through grants to independent nonprofits, plus a tenant outreach program, and lets tenant groups take part in inspections — adding units they flag, meeting inspectors, and reviewing management records.
Keeps rental assistance attached to units during foreclosure and property disposition so tenants do not lose their subsidy when a building changes hands.

analysis.who_pays: Owners and managers of HUD-assisted multifamily buildings pay: their subsidies can be withheld, their rent increases frozen, their buildings taken over by the Secretary in extreme cases, and their financial dealings with HUD opened to tenant associations. They also face tenant-initiated inspections and federally funded organizing on their properties. HUD and public housing agencies bear the administrative cost of the new enforcement, escrow, and inspection procedures.

drawbacks.text: Withholding housing assistance payments and letting tenants pay into escrow could squeeze owners' cash flow, which for some smaller or financially fragile owners could worsen building upkeep in the short term rather than fix it.

The bill creates significant new administrative work for HUD and local public housing agencies — expedited enforcement determinations, negotiated staged escrow releases, environmental testing, and expanded inspection procedures — with no dedicated funding for those agency costs.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For tenants, the benefits are substantial and concrete: a way to force repairs without losing their homes, and leverage — withheld federal money — to make landlords act. The costs fall on owners of federally assisted properties, who would face withheld subsidy payments, tenant-initiated inspections, forced financial disclosure, and federally funded tenant organizing, plus administrative costs for HUD and local housing agencies. An honest supporter would acknowledge the repair-and-deduct and escrow mechanisms could be cumbersome in practice and that shifting management to the Secretary in extreme cases is a heavy intervention; but the bill's core bargain — federal dollars should not subsidize hazardous housing — is a defensible one.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Financial Services Committee the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, markup, or vote before the 118th Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on June 28, 2024, near the end of a two-year Congress, and referred the same day to the House Committee on Financial Services.
No further action was ever taken: no hearing, no committee vote, no floor vote. When the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, the bill died there.
Its 17 cosponsors were all Democrats, and the bill was never reported out of a committee controlled by the opposing party.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Owners of federally subsidized apartment buildings are better off: no new enforcement powers for tenants, no withheld subsidies, and no mandated disclosure of their finances took effect. Tenants living in problem buildings are no better off than before.

industries.industry: Owners and operators of HUD-assisted multifamily housing
industries.note: The bill would let HUD withhold their subsidies, freeze their rents, seize management of failing buildings, expose their finances to tenant groups, and fund independent tenant organizing against them. Its core bargain is that federal rent subsidies stop flowing to owners who let their buildings fall apart.

industries.industry: Rural rental housing owners with USDA Section 515 agreements
industries.note: The bill's enforcement provisions extend to USDA rural rental housing agreements, subjecting those owners to the same tenant petition and court-enforcement remedies.

industries.industry: Tenant organizing and housing nonprofit groups
industries.note: The bill channels federal grants to independent nonprofits for tenant outreach, training, and capacity building, and requires grant recipients to be independent of landlords. It also creates paid-for predevelopment assistance enabling transfers of buildings to tenant, nonprofit, or public owners.
